opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually quite natural. When a capability becomes clearly valuable and clearly measurable, everyone rushes toward it, and coding is exactly that kind of domain. Code has a verifier built in: you can run it, test it, and see whether it works. That makes it an ideal training ground for reinforcement learning and for agents that take many steps toward a goal. There's also a direct business case, since developers are willing to pay and the productivity gains show up immediately. So I'm not surprised so many companies converge there.

But I'd make two points. First, homogeneous competition isn't necessarily bad. It drives the technology forward very quickly, and the lessons we learn from agentic coding, like long-horizon planning, tool use, and self-correction, will transfer to many other areas. In some sense coding is the first place where agents really work, and it's teaching the whole field how to build them.

Second, I think the bigger frontier is somewhere else. Coding lives entirely in the digital world. Much of the economy, and much of what matters to people, happens in the physical world: manufacturing, logistics, robots, autonomous vehicles. For AI to help there, it needs to understand physics, space, and cause and effect, not just text and code. That's why I spend so much time thinking about world models and physical AI. The data is harder to get, verification is harder, and progress is slower, which is exactly why fewer people are crowding into it. To me, the long-term differentiation will come less from who builds the slightly better coding agent and more from who can bring intelligence into the physical world.

So competition in coding is healthy and expected. But if everyone works on the same thing, some important problems get underexplored, and I'd encourage more people to take on those harder, less crowded directions.

r001.rationale: The response discusses coding’s value and the appeal of physical AI, but does not cite avoiding dependence on another company for core technology as a reason to compete on coding.

r002.rationale: It says long-term differentiation will come from bringing intelligence into the physical world, beyond building a better coding agent, suggesting companies have other ways to differentiate.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's natural, and honestly I don't worry about it too much. When a new technology arrives, everyone rushes to the most obvious application first, and coding is the most obvious one because the feedback loop is so clean. Code either runs or it doesn't. You can verify it, you can generate training data from it, the users are the same people building the models. So of course everyone converges there. That's not a sign of a lack of imagination, it's a sign that the signal is strong.

But I'd say two things. First, homogeneous competition at the beginning doesn't mean homogeneous outcomes at the end. In every wave, the early period looks crowded, and then the winners separate based on things that aren't visible yet: distribution, how deeply you integrate into workflows, how much you actually understand the user's job rather than just the benchmark. Coding agents today all look similar on a demo. They won't look similar after two years of people living with them.

Second, and this is where my own bias shows, I think the bigger opportunity is actually in what comes after coding. Coding is the easy world for agents, because the world is digital and fully observable. The hard world is the physical world. Robots, factories, autonomous machines, anything that has to deal with physics, with partial information, with consequences you can't undo by hitting Ctrl-Z. Very few companies are seriously working on that, because the data is scarce and the feedback loop is slow. That's precisely why I find it interesting. If everyone is in one room, the room next door is empty.

So my view is: if you're a startup and your whole story is "we also do agentic coding," you should be nervous, because you're competing against people with more compute and more distribution. But if you treat coding as the proving ground for agent capabilities and then take those capabilities somewhere harder, the competition in coding is actually your friend. It's driving down the cost of the underlying models for everyone.

r001.rationale: The candidate says coding attracts companies because it is an obvious application with clean feedback and strong signals. It does not identify avoiding dependence on another company for core technology as a reason to compete.

r002.rationale: The candidate says early competition does not determine the eventual winners, which will separate through distribution, workflow integration, and understanding users’ jobs. It also describes moving capabilities beyond coding as an opportunity to differentiate.

astra-6.text:
I think some convergence is natural. Coding is a valuable application, and it has a relatively clear feedback loop: you can run the code, test it, and see whether it works. So it makes sense that many companies are investing in it.

But working on the same category doesn’t necessarily mean building the same product. An agent that helps an individual write a small program is quite different from one that can work reliably in a large, existing codebase. Understanding context, making changes across multiple files, and verifying those changes—there’s still a lot to solve.

The question is whether a company has a distinct insight into what users need. If everyone is just matching the latest feature, competition becomes very difficult. But if you can consistently solve a problem better, there’s room to create value even in a crowded market.

So I wouldn’t judge it just by how many companies are working on coding. I’d look at whether their products are becoming more useful and whether they have a credible path to differentiation.

r001.rationale: The response discusses coding’s clear feedback loop and competitive value, but does not mention avoiding dependence on another company for core technology.

r002.rationale: It says companies in the same category can build different products and points to distinct user insights and a credible path to differentiation beyond matching features.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s natural that many companies are focusing on coding. There’s a clear need, the results are relatively easy to evaluate, and better coding capabilities can also make agents more useful. So even if everyone is working in the same direction, that doesn’t necessarily mean they’ll end up building the same thing.

The question is where the differentiation comes from. Is your system more reliable? Can it understand a large codebase, work through a longer task, and verify that its changes actually solve the problem? There’s a big difference between generating a piece of code and completing useful work with very little supervision.

So I wouldn’t judge the competition just by how similar the demos look. I’d look at how much value the products deliver in real workflows. If everyone builds something interchangeable, competition will be difficult. But there’s still a lot of room to make these systems substantially better.

r001.rationale: The response discusses coding demand and product differentiation, but does not mention avoiding dependence on another company for core technology.

r002.rationale: It says companies may not build the same thing and points to reliability, handling large codebases, longer tasks, and verification as ways to differentiate beyond the shared focus on coding.
